title: Getting Oriented
answer: The first four chapters lay the foundation for everything that follows. They explain what AI can and cannot do, the ten patterns that account for nearly every idea in the Volume, the laws and rules that protect students, and a simple method for piloting and measuring any new tool.

children.name: What AI Can and Cannot Do
children.blurb: In the fall of 2023, nearly 1,000 students at a high school in Turkey took part in a simple test. During math review sessions, some students practiced with a plain AI chat tool, much like the free chatbots anyone can open on a phone.

children.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere
children.blurb: When this Volume began, the raw material was a stack of 1,200 ideas for using AI in schools, gathered from teachers, district leaders, researchers, and product lists. Reading them one by one felt like walking through a crowded market where every stall sold something slightly different.

children.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule
children.blurb: In June 2026, a school board member in Portland, Oregon, raised concerns about the data an AI reading assessment company would collect from students. The list of data fields in the company's contract included items such as place of birth and migrant status (Willamette Week, 2026).

children.name: Pilot, Measure, Scale
children.blurb: In a recent trial in Germany, 371 students in grades 7 through 9 used generative AI tools during six regular physics and English lessons. Some students got a tool designed to build motivation, some got a tool designed to teach learning strategies, and a comparison group used a plain chatbot.

sections.body: This opening part of the book is the foundation for everything else in the Volume, and it covers what AI can and cannot do, the ten patterns that account for nearly every idea in the book, the laws and rules that protect students, and a simple method for piloting and measuring any new tool. AI in this part is not yet doing a job in a classroom. It is being explained, bounded and placed under rules before anyone uses it. The book treats this orientation as the ground on which every later idea stands, and it says readers who start nowhere else should start here.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: What works, according to the book, is starting with the limits of AI and with the ten patterns that show up everywhere, because those patterns account for nearly every idea in the Volume. What also works is putting the laws and rules that protect students first, and using a simple method to pilot and measure any new tool before trusting it. What does not work is skipping this ground and going straight to tools, because the rules set out in these chapters apply to every idea in the chapters that follow. The rule the book holds to is that the foundation comes before the tool, and that protection and measurement come before scale.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The four pages fit together as a sequence from understanding to protection to testing. What AI Can and Cannot Do gives a teacher, leader or parent the plain limits of the technology, and Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere gives them the recurring ideas that explain almost everything later in the Volume. Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule is where a leader or parent goes for the laws and rules that protect students, and Pilot, Measure, Scale is where a teacher or leader goes for the simple method of trying a tool and checking it before spreading it. Read in that order, the pages move a reader from what the technology is, to what it keeps doing, to what must guard it, to how to test it.
